notes.meaning: Joshua calls all the tribes and leaders of Israel together at Shechem for a final gathering. This location was sacred because God first promised the land to Abraham here, and Jacob had buried household idols under an oak nearby. Presenting themselves 'before God' showed that the people met with deep reverence, as if standing right in the Lord's presence.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often note that this gathering begins a renewal ceremony structured like an ancient Near Eastern treaty, where a ruler presents his past kindness before asking for loyalty.

notes.meaning: Joshua speaks as a prophet, delivering God's own account of Israel's origin. Long ago, Abraham's family lived beyond the Euphrates River and worshiped idols just like their neighbors. God reminded them of this humble past to show that their nation existed entirely by His unearned grace, not because of their own goodness.

The Lord reminds the people that He personally led Abraham out of his homeland and guided him safely across Canaan. God miraculously gave him Isaac, and later gave Isaac two sons, Jacob and Esau. Esau received Mount Seir as his territory, while Jacob's family moved to Egypt, reserving the Promised Land specifically for Jacob's offspring.

God sent Moses and Aaron to confront Pharaoh and struck Egypt with terrible plagues. After breaking the power of their oppressors, the Lord brought Israel out of bitter slavery. Israel's story began with God saving them when they were completely unable to save themselves.

When the Egyptian army chased the fleeing Israelites with chariots and trapped them at the Red Sea, the people cried to the Lord in terror. God placed a dark cloud between the two camps for protection, brought the sea crashing down on the Egyptians, and watched over Israel during forty years in the desert. Some of the older men standing before Joshua had witnessed these miracles with their own eyes.

When Israel arrived east of the Jordan River, the Amorite kings marched out to attack them. The Lord gave Israel complete victory and handed over the territory so they could make it their home. This triumph proved that God's strength, not human military power, gave them the land.

Balak, the king of Moab, tried to defeat Israel by paying the prophet Balaam to place a spiritual curse on them. However, God refused to listen to Balaam and made him speak words of blessing instead. The Lord shielded His people from spiritual malice just as He had protected them from enemy armies.

Israel crossed over the Jordan River and approached Jericho, where seven different Canaanite nations stood against them. Even though these groups were fierce and well fortified, the Lord delivered every one of them into Israel's hands. The conquest succeeded because God was fulfilling the promises He had made long before.

The Lord drove out the Amorite kings ahead of Israel, reminding them that their victory did not come from their own swords or bows. Now they lived in cities they had never spent time building and ate from olive groves and vineyards they had never planted. Their entire inheritance was a generous gift of divine grace.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars view the 'hornet' as a poetic figure of speech representing the overwhelming dread and panic God cast into the hearts of Israel's enemies.

notes.meaning: In light of all God has done, Joshua commands the people to revere Him and serve Him with sincere, honest hearts. He tells them to cast away every household idol their ancestors carried from Mesopotamia or kept in Egypt. Loving God requires cleaning out false loyalties so that He alone receives worship.

Joshua urges the people to make an open, definite decision about who has their devotion. They can worship the ancient gods of their ancestors or the local gods of Canaan, but they must make up their minds. Joshua then speaks for his own family, declaring that no matter what the rest of the nation does, he and his household will serve the Lord.

differ.view: Pastors in this tradition often use Joshua's pledge to highlight the father's biblical duty to lead his home in regular family worship and spiritual instruction.

notes.meaning: The people shudder at the thought of abandoning the Lord to chase after other gods. They recall how He delivered them from Egyptian slavery, shielded them through their long journey, and drove out their enemies. Because of His undeniable goodness and rescue, they eagerly promise that they will serve Him alone.

Joshua startles the crowd by telling them they are unable to serve God purely on their own strength. God is completely holy and jealous for their whole heart, meaning He will not overlook willful rebellion or tolerate rivals. If they make cheap promises and later turn to idols, the very God who blessed them will bring severe judgment upon them.

Even after Joshua warns them about how demanding God's covenant is, the people refuse to back down. They insist that they will remain faithful and serve only the Lord. Joshua's warning accomplished its purpose by forcing them to count the cost of true obedience.

Joshua reminds the people that their own words will act as evidence against them. If they ever turn away from the Lord, their public promise will stand in court to convict them. The people readily accept this responsibility, agreeing that they are witnesses to their own vow.

Joshua tells them to prove their sincerity immediately by throwing out any hidden foreign idols and turning their hearts fully to the God of Israel. The people respond with a third promise, confirming that they will obey the Lord's voice in all things. True faith always shows itself by actively clearing away temptations and seeking God's will.

Joshua seals this commitment that day at Shechem, officially renewing Israel's sacred covenant with God. He establishes clear rules and reminders to guide their daily life with the Lord. This agreement firmly bound the people to the commands Moses had originally given them.

Joshua writes down the words of the covenant in the official Book of the Law of God so they will never be forgotten. He also places a large stone under an oak tree near the sanctuary as a permanent physical reminder. Figuratively speaking, the stone is said to have 'heard' their vows so that it would stand as a silent witness against them if they ever proved unfaithful.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Treaties across the ancient Near East commonly set up stones or natural markers as lasting witnesses to remind future generations of a sacred oath.

notes.meaning: With the covenant renewed and recorded, Joshua sends the people away. Each tribe and family returns in peace to their allotted land. Joshua's public ministry concludes with Israel firmly pledged to follow God.

Sometime after this gathering, Joshua dies at the age of 110, honored with the noble title 'the servant of the LORD.' The people lay him to rest on his own family property at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. Joshua's life stands as an example of quiet, lifelong obedience to God rather than a quest for personal fame.

Israel continued to worship and obey the Lord throughout Joshua's lifetime and during the lives of the older leaders who outlived him. These elders had seen firsthand the astonishing miracles God performed to deliver and settle the nation. Godly leadership leaves a powerful heritage that can preserve a community in faith for many years.

The Israelites finally bury the bones of Joseph at Shechem, on the piece of ground Jacob had purchased centuries before. Carrying Joseph's remains out of Egypt through forty years in the wilderness honored his dying request and demonstrated their faith in God's promises. This burial proved that God faithfully brings His people home just as He said.

Eleazar the high priest, who had partnered with Joshua to guide the nation, passes away and is buried at Gibeah in the hills of Ephraim. His passing marks the final departure of the generation that led Israel into the Promised Land. With these trusted leaders gone, Israel was left with God's word and the duty to stay faithful on their own.
